1	---
     2	title: Making the case for Maester
     3	description: Templates to explain to executives, a CISO and an IT Security Adviser why your organisation should monitor its Microsoft 365 configuration with Maester, with examples of what goes unnoticed without it.
     4	---
     5	
     6	import { Tabs, TabItem } from '@astrojs/starlight/components';
     7	
     8	# Making the case for Maester
     9	
    10	Maester is free, but rolling it out still needs someone's time, a place to run it and, often, approval. This page
    11	helps you get that approval. It has three parts:
    12	
    13	1. [What organisations miss without continuous monitoring](#what-organisations-miss-without-continuous-monitoring):
    14	   real configuration failures, each with the Maester test that catches it. Use them as examples in any of the
    15	   templates.
    16	2. [Templates](#templates) for three audiences: general executives, a CISO, and an IT Security Adviser (ITSA). Copy
    17	   one, replace the text in `[brackets]`, and delete what does not apply.
    18	3. [Common questions](#common-questions) that come up in these conversations, with honest answers.
    19	
    20	:::tip[Run Maester first]
    21	The strongest argument is your own tenant. Run Maester once (see [Getting started](getting-started.mdx)) and quote
    22	your own numbers: how many Critical and High failures there are, and two or three examples from the list below that
    23	you actually found.
    24	:::
    25	
    26	## What organisations miss without continuous monitoring
    27	
    28	A Microsoft 365 tenant changes every week: people join and leave, admins grant exceptions, projects add apps, and
    29	Microsoft releases new features with new settings. Most security weaknesses in a tenant are not the result of an
    30	attack. They are a setting that was right once, and was then changed, or quietly stopped working, without anyone
    31	noticing. A yearly audit or a one-off assessment sees the tenant on one day. Continuous monitoring sees the day it
    32	changed.
    33	
    34	| What goes wrong | Why nobody notices | What it can lead to | Maester checks |
    35	| --- | --- | --- | --- |
    36	| **A Conditional Access policy stops protecting anyone.** The group it targets is deleted, or a user or role it names no longer exists. | The policy still shows as *On* in the portal. Nothing alerts. | Users who should need MFA, or a compliant device, sign in without either. | [MT.1038](/docs/tests/MT.1038), [MT.1066](/docs/tests/MT.1066) |
    37	| **Admins lock themselves out.** An emergency access (break glass) account is caught by a new policy, or blocked. | The account is used only in an emergency, so the problem is found during the emergency. | No way into the tenant during an outage or an incident. | [MT.1005](/docs/tests/MT.1005), [MT.1034](/docs/tests/MT.1034) |
    38	| **Too many people hold the keys.** Global Administrators accumulate; people who left or changed role keep privileged roles. | Role assignments are rarely reviewed, and each one was justified when it was made. | A single phished account can take over the whole tenant. | [MT.1032](/docs/tests/MT.1032), [MT.1029](/docs/tests/MT.1029), [CIS.M365.1.1.3](/docs/tests/CIS.M365.1.1.3) |
    39	| **MFA is bypassed through legacy authentication.** An exception is added for an old device or app and never removed. | MFA appears to be enforced for everyone. | Password spraying succeeds against accounts that "have MFA". | [MT.1009](/docs/tests/MT.1009), [CISA.MS.AAD.1.1](/docs/tests/CISA.MS.AAD.1.1) |
    40	| **Users hand attackers access through an app.** Users can consent to third-party apps that read mail and files. | Consent looks like a normal sign-in prompt to the user. | Persistent access to mailboxes and files that survives a password reset. | [CIS.M365.5.1.5.1](/docs/tests/CIS.M365.5.1.5.1), [EIDSCA.AP08](/docs/tests/EIDSCA.AP08) |
    41	| **Mail is forwarded outside the organisation.** Automatic forwarding to external domains is allowed. | Forwarding rules are set per mailbox, often by an attacker after a compromise. | Silent, continuing data loss. | [CISA.MS.EXO.1.1](/docs/tests/CISA.MS.EXO.1.1) |
    42	| **There is no record when you need it.** Audit logging or mailbox auditing is off. | Logs are only looked at after an incident. | You cannot tell what an attacker did, or meet breach-notification and legal obligations. | [CIS.M365.3.1.1](/docs/tests/CIS.M365.3.1.1), [CISA.MS.EXO.13.1](/docs/tests/CISA.MS.EXO.13.1) |
    43	| **Anyone can send email as you.** DMARC is missing or not enforced on a domain. | Mail still flows normally. | Invoice fraud and phishing that appears to come from your own domain. | [MT.1182](/docs/tests/MT.1182) |
    44	| **Applications hold powerful, long-lived secrets.** A service principal with a client secret holds a permanent privileged role. | Apps are created by projects and rarely reviewed by security. | A leaked secret gives an attacker admin rights without any user sign-in or MFA. | [MT.1027](/docs/tests/MT.1027), [MT.1057](/docs/tests/MT.1057) |
    45	| **An integration stops working.** An app registration's certificate or secret expires. | The expiry date is in the portal, but nobody is watching it. | An outage of a business process that depends on the app. | [MT.1199](/docs/tests/MT.1199) (long-running: add `-IncludeLongRunning`) |
    46	| **Files are shared with anyone.** External sharing is opened up for one project and left open. | Sharing settings are changed in a different admin centre from the rest of security. | Sensitive documents reachable by people outside the organisation. | [CIS.M365.7.2.3](/docs/tests/CIS.M365.7.2.3) |
    47	| **A new phishing technique works.** Device code sign-in is allowed for everyone. | It is on by default and rarely needed. | Phishing that captures a signed-in session, including MFA. | [CIS.M365.5.2.2.12](/docs/tests/CIS.M365.5.2.2.12) |
    48	
    49	Beyond individual weaknesses, an organisation without continuous monitoring also misses:
    50	
    51	- **Early warning.** A weakening change is found within a day, by your team, instead of months later by an auditor,
    52	  a penetration tester or an attacker.
    53	- **Evidence on demand.** Every run is a dated, repeatable record of which controls passed. Audit and assurance
    54	  evidence no longer has to be gathered by hand.
    55	- **Knowledge that stays when people leave.** Your intent ("this group must always be in this policy") is written
    56	  down as a test, not kept in one admin's head.
    57	- **A measurable trend.** You can report the number of open Critical and High findings each month, and show it
    58	  going down.
    59	- **Safe change.** Admins can make changes with the confidence that a mistake will be caught by the next run.
    60	
    61	## Templates
    62	
    63	<Tabs syncKey="audience">
    64	<TabItem label="General executives">
    65	
    66	Keep this to one page. Executives want to know the risk, the cost and what you need from them. Avoid product names
    67	and technical terms beyond the first mention.
    68	
    69	---
    70	
    71	**To:** [Name, role]
    72	**From:** [Your name, role]
    73	**Subject:** Continuous checks on our Microsoft 365 security settings
    74	
    75	**Summary**
    76	
    77	Our email, files, Teams and user sign-ins run on Microsoft 365. Its security depends on hundreds of settings, and
    78	those settings change every week as people join and leave and as we add new services. Today we check them
    79	[once a year during the audit / when something goes wrong / not at all]. I propose that we check them automatically
    80	every day with Maester, a free tool used by [organisations like ours], so that we find a weakening change within a day
    81	instead of at the next audit or after an incident.
    82	
    83	**Why this matters**
    84	
    85	Most security weaknesses in cloud services are not caused by sophisticated attacks. They are caused by a setting
    86	that was changed, or stopped working, without anyone noticing. For example:
    87	
    88	- [A sign-in protection that appears to be on but no longer covers anyone, because the group it applied to was deleted.]
    89	- [Our own example from the first run: "We found [number] accounts with full administrator rights; we expected [number]."]
    90	- [An example from the list above that applies to us.]
    91	
    92	Any one of these can lead to [a data breach / fraudulent payments from spoofed email / an outage of a business
    93	system / a failed audit].
    94	
    95	**What we propose**

    26	## What organisations miss without continuous monitoring
    27	
    28	A Microsoft 365 tenant changes every week: people join and leave, admins grant exceptions, projects add apps, and
    29	Microsoft releases new features with new settings. Most security weaknesses in a tenant are not the result of an
    30	attack. They are a setting that was right once, and was then changed, or quietly stopped working, without anyone
    31	noticing. A yearly audit or a one-off assessment sees the tenant on one day. Continuous monitoring sees the day it
    32	changed.
    33	
    34	| What goes wrong | Why nobody notices | What it can lead to | Maester checks |
    35	| --- | --- | --- | --- |
    36	| **A Conditional Access policy stops protecting anyone.** The group it targets is deleted, or a user or role it names no longer exists. | The policy still shows as *On* in the portal. Nothing alerts. | Users who should need MFA, or a compliant device, sign in without either. | [MT.1038](/docs/tests/MT.1038), [MT.1066](/docs/tests/MT.1066) |
    37	| **Admins lock themselves out.** An emergency access (break glass) account is caught by a new policy, or blocked. | The account is used only in an emergency, so the problem is found during the emergency. | No way into the tenant during an outage or an incident. | [MT.1005](/docs/tests/MT.1005), [MT.1034](/docs/tests/MT.1034) |
    38	| **Too many people hold the keys.** Global Administrators accumulate; people who left or changed role keep privileged roles. | Role assignments are rarely reviewed, and each one was justified when it was made. | A single phished account can take over the whole tenant. | [MT.1032](/docs/tests/MT.1032), [MT.1029](/docs/tests/MT.1029), [CIS.M365.1.1.3](/docs/tests/CIS.M365.1.1.3) |
    39	| **MFA is bypassed through legacy authentication.** An exception is added for an old device or app and never removed. | MFA appears to be enforced for everyone. | Password spraying succeeds against accounts that "have MFA". | [MT.1009](/docs/tests/MT.1009), [CISA.MS.AAD.1.1](/docs/tests/CISA.MS.AAD.1.1) |
    40	| **Users hand attackers access through an app.** Users can consent to third-party apps that read mail and files. | Consent looks like a normal sign-in prompt to the user. | Persistent access to mailboxes and files that survives a password reset. | [CIS.M365.5.1.5.1](/docs/tests/CIS.M365.5.1.5.1), [EIDSCA.AP08](/docs/tests/EIDSCA.AP08) |
    41	| **Mail is forwarded outside the organisation.** Automatic forwarding to external domains is allowed. | Forwarding rules are set per mailbox, often by an attacker after a compromise. | Silent, continuing data loss. | [CISA.MS.EXO.1.1](/docs/tests/CISA.MS.EXO.1.1) |
    42	| **There is no record when you need it.** Audit logging or mailbox auditing is off. | Logs are only looked at after an incident. | You cannot tell what an attacker did, or meet breach-notification and legal obligations. | [CIS.M365.3.1.1](/docs/tests/CIS.M365.3.1.1), [CISA.MS.EXO.13.1](/docs/tests/CISA.MS.EXO.13.1) |
    43	| **Anyone can send email as you.** DMARC is missing or not enforced on a domain. | Mail still flows normally. | Invoice fraud and phishing that appears to come from your own domain. | [MT.1182](/docs/tests/MT.1182) |
    44	| **Applications hold powerful, long-lived secrets.** A service principal with a client secret holds a permanent privileged role. | Apps are created by projects and rarely reviewed by security. | A leaked secret gives an attacker admin rights without any user sign-in or MFA. | [MT.1027](/docs/tests/MT.1027), [MT.1057](/docs/tests/MT.1057) |

   218	  limited by an Exchange role such as View-Only Configuration.
   219	- For the SharePoint tests: an app registration with `AllSites.FullControl` (delegated) or `Sites.FullControl.All`
   220	  (unattended). The tests only read, but the permission would allow changes, so treat this identity as privileged.
   221	  [We will / will not run the SharePoint tests.]
   222	- Unattended runs use [a workload identity with federated credentials / a managed identity / a certificate], with no
   223	  stored secret [where possible]. See [Monitoring with Maester](monitoring/readme.mdx).
   224	
   225	**Where it runs and where data goes**
   226	
   227	- Runs in [our GitHub Actions / Azure DevOps / Azure Automation / an admin workstation], in [region / environment].
   228	- Results (HTML, JSON, optional CSV and Excel) are written to [storage location], with access limited to [group].
   229	  They describe our security configuration and should be classified as [classification].
   230	- User identities can be replaced in every output with `-RedactUserIdentity AllOutputs`. `HtmlOnly` redacts only
   231	  the HTML report, so the JSON, CSV and other machine-readable outputs keep the real identifiers. Redaction is best
   232	  effort and can miss names in free text. It is pseudonymisation, not anonymisation: each user is replaced by a token
   233	  derived from an unsalted hash of their identity, so anyone who can guess a user's user principal name or object ID
   234	  can confirm it. See [Hiding user identities from reports](export-results.md#hiding-user-identities-from-reports).
   235	- By default the results include the list of affected objects (the users, policies and apps behind each finding).
   236	  `-ExcludeAffectedObjects` leaves it out.
   237	- Results are sent only where we configure them: [email recipients / a Teams channel / none].
   238	- Telemetry: by default each run sends a start and an end event to `api.maester.dev`, run by the Maester
   239	  maintainers. They hold a hash of our tenant ID and the number of tests that passed, failed or were skipped, never
   240	  which tests or what they found. For now each run also sends a legacy usage event, which holds our tenant ID, to
   241	  PostHog. See [What telemetry does Maester send?](faq.md#what-telemetry-does-maester-send). We will turn both off
   242	  with `-DisableTelemetry`. [Yes / No]
   243	- With `-SkipVersionCheck` the module makes no calls to check for a newer version.
   244	
   245	**Supply chain**
   246	
   247	- Source code is public and reviewed through pull requests; each test is a readable PowerShell file.
   248	- We will pin a specific module version, review release notes before upgrading, and install from [the PowerShell
   249	  Gallery / our internal repository].
   250	- Optional Maester Packs are third-party code and are not installed unless we install them. [We will not use packs /
   251	  we will use only (pack) after review.]
   252	
   253	**Residual risks and mitigations**
   254	
   255	| Risk | Mitigation |
   256	| --- | --- |
   257	| The monitoring identity is compromised and used to read the tenant's configuration | Read-only Graph permissions (plus the SharePoint and optional permissions above, if used), [federated credential / certificate in Key Vault], sign-in monitoring on the identity, Conditional Access for workload identities [if licensed] |
   258	| Reports disclose our security weaknesses | Access-controlled storage, redaction of user identities, retention of [N days] |
   259	| A malicious or faulty module release | Version pinning, review before upgrade, [internal repository] |
   260	| False assurance from passing tests | Maester tests configuration only; it complements, and does not replace, [penetration testing / SIEM / audit] |
   261	
   262	**Request**
   263	
   264	Assessment and approval to run Maester [version] with the access above, from [environment], by [date].
   265	
   266	---
   267	
   268	</TabItem>
   269	</Tabs>
   270	
   271	## Common questions
   272	
   273	**We already have Microsoft Secure Score. Why add this?**
   274	Secure Score is Microsoft's view of recommended settings, and it is worth tracking. Maester adds what Secure Score
   275	does not: tests for your own rules (this group must be in this policy, this app must not have these permissions),
   276	results mapped to the framework you report against, a daily result in your own pipeline with alerts, and the
   277	CIS, CISA, ASD Essential Eight, EIDSCA and ORCA checks side by side with Maester's own.
   278	
   279	**We already have a SIEM, Defender and Sentinel.**
   280	Those watch for activity: sign-ins, alerts, attacks in progress. Maester checks configuration: whether the controls
   281	that prevent those attacks are still in place. A weak setting produces no alert until it is exploited.
   282	
   283	**It is free. Who supports it?**
   284	Maester is an open-source project maintained by a community of Microsoft security practitioners, with the source
   285	on [GitHub](https://github.com/maester365/maester). There is no vendor support contract. Because it only reads
   286	configuration and runs in your own environment, the operational risk of a fault is low: the worst case is a run that
   287	fails or a test that reports the wrong result, which you can turn off.
   288	
   289	**Will it change anything in our tenant?**
   290	Not by default: Maester asks only for read permissions. Two optional permissions are off unless you ask for them:
   291	sending mail, and `-Privileged`, which lets one test turn off report obfuscation while it runs and then turn it back
   292	on. The SharePoint tests need a full-control SharePoint permission, although they only read.
   293	
   294	**How much work is it?**
   295	A first report takes about fifteen minutes. Scheduled monitoring takes a few hours to set up with one of the
   296	[monitoring guides](monitoring/readme.mdx). The ongoing work is fixing what it finds, which is the point.
   297	
   298	**We will get hundreds of failures on the first run.**
   299	That is normal, and it is the reason to start. Fix Critical and High first, record the findings you accept as
   300	exceptions with a reason, and report the trend. See [Getting started](getting-started.mdx#step-3-fix-what-matters-first).

---
title: Installation guide
---

import InstallCommand from '@components/InstallCommand.astro';

Maester needs **PowerShell 7.4 or later** on Windows, Linux or macOS. Windows PowerShell 5.1 is not supported.

- Install the **Maester** PowerShell module.

<InstallCommand />

The tests ship inside the module, so there is nothing else to download and no folder to set up.

- Sign into your Microsoft 365 tenant and run the tests.

```powershell
Connect-Maester
Invoke-Maester
```

You only need a folder if you want to change settings or add your own tests. Put a `maester-config.json` (see [Configuration](configuration/overview.md)) and a `custom` folder for your tests (see [Writing custom tests](writing-tests/index.mdx)) in it, and run `Invoke-Maester -Path <folder>` or run Maester from that folder.

:::note[Pester]
Maester 3.0 does not need Pester. Install it only if you have custom tests written in the Pester format (`*.Tests.ps1`), see [Pester-format tests](writing-tests/pester-format-tests.md):

```powershell
Install-Module Pester -MinimumVersion 5.7.1 -SkipPublisherCheck -Force -Scope CurrentUser
```
:::

Upgrading from Maester 2.x? See [Upgrading from 2.x](upgrading-from-2x.md).

## Invoke-Maester

To learn more about the `Invoke-Maester` cmdlet including how to filter tests, see the [Invoke-Maester](commands/Invoke-Maester.mdx) documentation and the [run configuration reference](configuration/run-configuration.md).

content.text:
**It's nearly ready to merge. Three one-line wording fixes are left, and then it's good to go.** The pages are accurate, read well and are aimed at the right people.

## Do the docs make sense?

Yes. Each page has one clear job:

- **Getting started**: install → read the report → fix Critical/High first → config → baseline → monitor → custom tests. It's the path new users are missing today, and it links to the detailed pages instead of copying them. The results table (Passed / Failed / Investigate / Skipped / Error / Not run) is the most useful part.
- **Choosing a baseline**: it doesn't push one framework. The "If your requirement is… → Run" table is the right way in, and the section on how suites overlap answers a question people ask often.
- **Making the case**: the "what goes unnoticed" table is strong. The executive, CISO and ITSA templates are long, but they're tabbed and meant to be copied, so the length is fine. The ITSA template is unusually honest about SharePoint full control, `-Privileged`, the limits of redaction and telemetry. That will help it get through a security review.

## Fact check

I checked the pages against the code:
- **Test IDs:** all 24 cited exist and match what the pages say about them.
- **Switches:** every switch named exists on `Invoke-Maester`, `Connect-Maester` or `Get-MtGraphScope`.
- **Behaviour claims:**
  - MT.1076 really does turn report obfuscation off and back on.
  - MT.1199 is long-running.
  - MT.1198 has the `MaximumValidityDays` parameter.
  - The telemetry description matches `Write-Telemetry.ps1`.
  - The "Fix first" panel exists.
- **Your earlier review:** all six points were addressed.
- **CI:** green.

## Fix before merge

These are 3 of the 4 CodeRabbit threads still open from Nov 8. They were posted after the author's last push.
1. **`making-the-case.mdx:97`**: the executive template says Maester "does not change" settings, but the ITSA template and the FAQ say `-Privileged` does. Add "by default".
2. **`making-the-case.mdx:147`**: the CISO template says "read-only identity", but SharePoint needs full control. Qualify it so a CISO doesn't approve a narrower access than the one actually granted.
3. **`choosing-a-baseline.md:19`**: "Each requirement carries its NIST SP 800-53 references" isn't quite true. 8 of 79 CISA requirements have none, so change it to "where available".

The fourth thread (line 114) is just CodeRabbit running its own checks and doesn't ask for a change.

## Nice to have, not blocking

- **"Getting started" and "Installation" overlap.** They now sit next to each other in the sidebar, and both cover install → `Connect-Maester` → `Invoke-Maester` plus the config folder and `-Path`. The Installation page's "Next Steps" should point to Getting started so readers aren't sent in circles.
- **DISA STIG isn't in the suite table.** That's correct for now, because it isn't on main yet. Add a row when PR 2739 lands.
- **The ITSA template names PostHog.** It's accurate now, but it will need updating when PostHog is retired.

The local preview is still running at http://localhost:3278 if you want to read the pages yourself.

content.content:
## Optional modules and permissions

Maester includes optional [CISA](tests/cisa/) tests that require additional permissions and modules to run. These optional tests are skipped if the modules are not installed or there is no active connection.

> Also see [Create-entra-app](sections/create-entra-app.md)

### Installing Azure, Exchange Online, Teams and PnP.PowerShell modules

```powershell
Install-Module Az.Accounts, ExchangeOnlineManagement, MicrosoftTeams, PnP.PowerShell -Scope CurrentUser
```

> The Security & Compliance PowerShell module is dependent on the ExchangeOnlineManagement `Connect-IPPSSession` cmdlet.

### Connecting to Azure, Exchange, and other services

In order to run all the CISA tests, you need to connect to the Azure, Exchange Online, and other modules.

For a more detailed introduction to these concepts see the [Connect-Maester](connect-maester/readme.md) documentation.

Run the following command to interactively connect to the Azure, Microsoft Graph, Exchange Online, and other modules. A sign-in window will appear for each module.

```powershell
Connect-Maester -Service All
```

### Connecting to GitHub

GitHub is an optional connection for GitHub security tests and is not included in `Connect-Maester -Service All`.
For interactive sessions, use the Maester GitHub App OAuth flow:

```powershell
Connect-Maester -Service Graph,GitHub -GitHubOrganization '<github-organization>'
```

See [Connect to GitHub (optional)](connect-maester/readme.md#connect-to-github-optional) for GitHub App install/approval details and token-based automation options.

### Permissions

Exchange Online implements a [role-based access control model](https://learn.microsoft.com/exchange/permissions-exo/permissions-exo). The controls these cmdlets test require minimum roles of either of the following:

* View-Only Configuration OR
* O365SupportViewConfig

### Installing Azure DevOps PowerShell module

```powershell
Install-Module ADOPS -Scope CurrentUser
```

### Connecting to Azure DevOps

In order to run all the Azure DevOps tests, you need to connect to Azure DevOps.

This is currently not included as part of [Connect-Maester](connect-maester/readme.md) and must be called separately. Run the following command to interactively connect using the Azure DevOps modules. A sign-in window will appear.

Example with PowerShell variable
```powershell
$AdoPSAllowInsecureAPIs = $true
Import-Module ADOPS
Connect-ADOPS -Organization <Name Of DevOps Organization>
```

Example with ArgumentList
```powershell
Import-Module ADOPS -ArgumentList $true
Connect-ADOPS -Organization <Name Of DevOps Organization>
```

> Note: Some of the API endpoints used for Azure DevOps tests use unsupported endpoints.
To allow usage of unsupported endpoints, you must set `$true` in the argumentlist when importing the module, or set a PowerShell variable called "$AdoPSAllowInsecureAPIs" to `$true` before importing the module.
Reference: https://github.com/AZDOPS/AZDOPS/issues/248

### Permissions

Azure DevOps implements a [role-based access control model](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/devops/organizations/security/permissions?view=azure-devops&tabs=preview-page). The controls these cmdlets test require the minimum role of:

* Project-Scoped Users at Organization level

## Optional modules and permissions

Maester includes optional [CISA](tests/cisa/) tests that require additional permissions and modules to run. These optional tests are skipped if the modules are not installed or there is no active connection.

> Also see [Create-entra-app](sections/create-entra-app.md)

### Installing Azure, Exchange Online, Teams and PnP.PowerShell modules

```powershell
Install-Module Az.Accounts, ExchangeOnlineManagement, MicrosoftTeams, PnP.PowerShell -Scope CurrentUser
```

> The Security & Compliance PowerShell module is dependent on the ExchangeOnlineManagement `Connect-IPPSSession` cmdlet.

### Connecting to Azure, Exchange, and other services

In order to run all the CISA tests, you need to connect to the Azure, Exchange Online, and other modules.

For a more detailed introduction to these concepts see the [Connect-Maester](connect-maester/readme.md) documentation.

Run the following command to interactively connect to the Azure, Microsoft Graph, Exchange Online, and other modules. A sign-in window will appear for each module.

```powershell
Connect-Maester -Service All
```

### Connecting to GitHub

GitHub is an optional connection for GitHub security tests and is not included in `Connect-Maester -Service All`.
For interactive sessions, use the Maester GitHub App OAuth flow:

```powershell
Connect-Maester -Service Graph,GitHub -GitHubOrganization '<github-organization>'
```

See [Connect to GitHub (optional)](connect-maester/readme.md#connect-to-github-optional) for GitHub App install/approval details and token-based automation options.

### Permissions

Exchange Online implements a [role-based access control model](https://learn.microsoft.com/exchange/permissions-exo/permissions-exo). The controls these cmdlets test require minimum roles of either of the following:

* View-Only Configuration OR
* O365SupportViewConfig

### Installing Azure DevOps PowerShell module

```powershell
Install-Module ADOPS -Scope CurrentUser
```

### Connecting to Azure DevOps

In order to run all the Azure DevOps tests, you need to connect to Azure DevOps.

This is currently not included as part of [Connect-Maester](connect-maester/readme.md) and must be called separately. Run the following command to interactively connect using the Azure DevOps modules. A sign-in window will appear.

Example with PowerShell variable
```powershell
$AdoPSAllowInsecureAPIs = $true
Import-Module ADOPS
Connect-ADOPS -Organization <Name Of DevOps Organization>
```

Example with ArgumentList
```powershell
Import-Module ADOPS -ArgumentList $true
Connect-ADOPS -Organization <Name Of DevOps Organization>
```

> Note: Some of the API endpoints used for Azure DevOps tests use unsupported endpoints.
To allow usage of unsupported endpoints, you must set `$true` in the argumentlist when importing the module, or set a PowerShell variable called "$AdoPSAllowInsecureAPIs" to `$true` before importing the module.
Reference: https://github.com/AZDOPS/AZDOPS/issues/248

### Permissions

Azure DevOps implements a [role-based access control model](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/devops/organizations/security/permissions?view=azure-devops&tabs=preview-page). The controls these cmdlets test require the minimum role of:

* Project-Scoped Users at Organization level

### Connect to SharePoint Online (optional)

Maester includes SharePoint Online security tests that use the [PnP PowerShell](https://pnp.github.io/powershell/) module.

Install the PnP PowerShell module if you haven't already:

```powershell
Install-Module PnP.PowerShell -Scope CurrentUser
```

A dedicated Entra ID app registration configured for PnP interactive login is required. The easiest way to create one is to follow the official [PnP app registration guide](https://pnp.github.io/powershell/articles/registerapplication.html) and run `Register-PnPEntraIDAppForInteractiveLogin`, which outputs the **Client ID** you will supply to `-SharePointClientId`. For the Maester-specific SharePoint permission setup, see [Grant permissions to SharePoint Online](../sections/create-entra-app.md).


Connect to SharePoint Online together with Microsoft Graph (the admin URL is auto-discovered from your tenant's initial domain):

```powershell
Connect-Maester -Service Graph,SharePointOnline -SharePointClientId '<Client ID>'
```

If auto-discovery does not work (e.g. in government or custom-domain tenants), supply the admin URL explicitly:

```powershell
Connect-Maester -Service Graph,SharePointOnline -SharePointClientId '<Client ID>' -SharePointAdminUrl 'https://contoso-admin.sharepoint.com'
```

If the PnP PowerShell module is not installed or there is no active connection, all SharePoint Online tests are skipped automatically.

### Connect to Azure, Exchange Online, Copilot Studio and Teams
### Connect to Azure DevOps (optional)

Maester includes an *optional* set of Azure DevOps security tests (AZDO.*).
These tests require the community [`ADOPS`](https://www.powershellgallery.com/packages/ADOPS) PowerShell module and an active connection to your Azure DevOps organization.

Connecting to Azure DevOps is **not** part of `Connect-Maester` and must be done separately:

```powershell
Install-Module ADOPS -Scope CurrentUser
Connect-ADOPS -Organization <your-organization>
```

If the `ADOPS` module is not installed or there is no active connection, the Azure DevOps tests are skipped automatically.

See the [installation guide](../installation.md#installing-azure-devops-powershell-module) for prerequisites and permissions, and the [Azure DevOps tests for Maester](/blog/azuredevops-tests-for-maester) blog post for the full list of available tests.

content.text:
**We still need the URL, but not the page as it is now.** The content can shrink to a short reference page, because most of it repeats Getting started or the [Connect-Maester](website/docs/connect-maester/readme.md) docs.

## Why the page can't just be deleted
`/docs/installation` is the site's main entry point:
- The header's **Get started** button and **Install** link, and the homepage **Quickstart →** button, all point to it (`SiteLayout.astro`, `index.astro`).
- The 404 page and six docs pages link to it.
- It's covered by the URL contract check.

Those buttons should now point to `/docs/getting-started`.

## What's only in the install guide
| Content | Elsewhere? |
| --- | --- |
| Windows PowerShell 5.1 is not supported | No |
| Tests ship inside the module, no folder needed | No |
| Pester is only needed for Pester-format custom tests | No |
| One `Install-Module` line for the Az, Exchange, Teams and PnP modules | Only PnP and ADOPS appear in Connect-Maester |
| Security & Compliance PowerShell comes with the ExchangeOnlineManagement module | No |
| Exchange roles for interactive runs (View-Only Configuration / O365SupportViewConfig) | Only for app-only runs (Connect-Maester advanced page) |
| Azure DevOps: the `$AdoPSAllowInsecureAPIs` flag and the minimum role | No; the Connect-Maester page links here for them |
| Install, connect, run; the `-Path` folder; connecting to Exchange, Teams, SharePoint and GitHub | Yes, in Getting started or Connect-Maester |

## Stale or wrong today
- **Wrong framing:** it calls the optional modules "optional CISA tests". They serve the Exchange, Teams and SharePoint tests in every suite.
- **Missing SharePoint setup:** Getting started says Installation covers `-SharePointClientId`, but it doesn't mention it.
- **Broken anchors:** `sections/create-entra-app.mdx` links to two anchors that no longer exist (`#installing-azure-and-exchange-online-modules`, `#installing-azure-exchange-online-and-teams-modules`).

## Proposed rewrite
1. **Make Installation a short reference** with:
   - requirements (PowerShell 7.4, no 5.1);
   - install, update and pinning a version, which the ITSA template tells readers to do but no page shows how;
   - one table per service: module to install, link to its Connect-Maester section, minimum role;
   - the Pester note and the link to Upgrading from 2.x.

   The quickstart part goes; it links to Getting started instead.
2. **Move the Azure DevOps detail** (insecure-API flag and permission) into the Connect-Maester Azure DevOps section, and repoint the two links to it. The anchors `#permissions` and `#optional-modules-and-permissions` stay, so links from other pages still work.
3. **Point the header and homepage buttons** to `/docs/getting-started`.
4. **Fix the broken `create-entra-app` anchors.**

Step 3 only works once Getting started exists. So this either goes on PR 2678's branch, which is jusso-dev's, or in a follow-up PR after it merges.

### Connect to Azure, Exchange Online, Copilot Studio and Teams

`Connect-Maester` also provides options to connect to Azure, Copilot Studio (via the Dataverse API), Exchange Online and Teams for running tests that use the Azure PowerShell, Dataverse OData API, Exchange Online PowerShell or Teams PowerShell modules.

The `-All` switch can be used to connect to all the services used by the Maester tests. This includes Microsoft Graph, Azure, Copilot Studio (Dataverse), Exchange Online, Security Compliance, Microsoft Teams, and SharePoint Online.

If `-SharePointClientId` is not provided, the SharePoint Online connection is skipped.

```powershell
Connect-Maester -Service All
```

When it finishes, `Connect-Maester` shows a summary of each service it tried. A service is **Connected**, **Skipped** (for example, no Dataverse environment or no `-SharePointClientId`), **Failed** (with the first line of the error), or **Not installed** (with the command to install the module).

-------                ------     -------
Microsoft Graph        Connected  user@contoso.com
Azure                  Connected  user@contoso.com
Dataverse              Skipped    No environment found, set DataverseEnvironmentUrl in maester-config.json
Exchange Online        Connected  user@contoso.com
Security & Compliance  Connected  user@contoso.com
Microsoft Teams        Connected  user@contoso.com
SharePoint Online      Skipped    -SharePointClientId was not provided

For more details on each connection, run Connect-Maester with -Verbose.
```

Run `Connect-Maester -Verbose` to see the step-by-step messages for each connection, including the full error when a service fails.

If you need to connect to just a subset of the services you can specifiy them using the `-Service` parameter.

```powershell
Connect-Maester -Service Azure,Graph,Teams
```

content.content:
---
title: Active Directory Connection Troubleshooting
description: "Fix Active Directory connection errors in Maester: TLS modes (LDAPS and StartTLS), domain controller certificate problems, the Linux and macOS StartTLS limit, and verbose diagnostics."
sidebar:
  label: AD Connection Troubleshooting
  order: 3
---
## Overview
- Maester uses System.DirectoryServices.Protocols.LdapConnection for cross-platform AD connectivity.
- TLS is required for all AD connections.
## Understanding TLS Modes
- The -ActiveDirectoryTlsMode parameter supports three values: Auto, Ldaps, StartTls.
- Auto (default): Tries LDAPS (port 636) first, then StartTLS (port 389) on Windows. On Linux/macOS, only tries LDAPS.
- Ldaps: Uses LDAPS on port 636 only.
- StartTls: Uses StartTLS on port 389 only.
- Auto mode adapts to the platform due to a known .NET limitation.
## Certificate Issues on the Domain Controller
- Common symptoms: connection fails with certificate, trust, validation, expired, or chain errors.
- Troubleshooting steps:
  1. Verify the DC has a valid server-authentication certificate installed.
  2. Verify the certificate SAN includes the DC's FQDN.
  3. Verify the certificate is not expired.
  4. On the client, verify the DC's certificate chain is trusted.
  5. For test environments only: use `Connect-Maester -Service ActiveDirectory -ActiveDirectorySkipCertificateCheck` to bypass certificate validation.
- If LDAPS fails but StartTLS succeeds, the DC's LDAPS certificate (port 636) is misconfigured — check the certificate on the DC.

---
title: Installation guide
description: What Maester needs, how to install, update and pin it, and the extra modules each service's tests use.
---

import InstallCommand from '@components/InstallCommand.astro';

This page is the reference for installing Maester and the modules its tests use. To go from nothing to your first
report, follow [Getting started](getting-started.mdx).

## Requirements

- **PowerShell 7.4 or later** on Windows, Linux or macOS. Windows PowerShell 5.1 is not supported.
- An account that can read your tenant's configuration, such as Global Reader. See
  [Connect-Maester](connect-maester/readme.md).

## Install Maester

<InstallCommand />

The tests ship inside the module, so there is nothing else to download and no folder to set up. Maester installs
`Microsoft.Graph.Authentication`, the only module it requires, with it.

You need a folder only to change settings or add your own tests. Put a `maester-config.json` (see

title: Installation guide
---

import InstallCommand from '@components/InstallCommand.astro';

Maester needs **PowerShell 7.4 or later** on Windows, Linux or macOS. Windows PowerShell 5.1 is not supported.

- Install the **Maester** PowerShell module.

<InstallCommand />

The tests ship inside the module, so there is nothing else to download and no folder to set up.

- Sign into your Microsoft 365 tenant and run the tests.

```powershell
Connect-Maester
Invoke-Maester
```

You only need a folder if you want to change settings or add your own tests. Put a `maester-config.json` (see [Configuration](configuration/overview.md)) and a `custom` folder for your tests (see [Writing custom tests](writing-tests/index.mdx)) in it, and run `Invoke-Maester -Path <folder>` or run Maester from that folder.

:::note[Pester]
Maester 3.0 does not need Pester. Install it only if you have custom tests written in the Pester format (`*.Tests.ps1`), see [Pester-format tests](writing-tests/pester-format-tests.md):

```powershell
Install-Module Pester -MinimumVersion 5.7.1 -SkipPublisherCheck -Force -Scope CurrentUser
```
:::

Upgrading from Maester 2.x? See [Upgrading from 2.x](upgrading-from-2x.md).

## Invoke-Maester

To learn more about the `Invoke-Maester` cmdlet including how to filter tests, see the [Invoke-Maester](commands/Invoke-Maester.mdx) documentation and the [run configuration reference](configuration/run-configuration.md).

## Optional modules and permissions

Maester includes optional [CISA](tests/cisa/) tests that require additional permissions and modules to run. These optional tests are skipped if the modules are not installed or there is no active connection.

> Also see [Create-entra-app](sections/create-entra-app.md)

### Installing Azure, Exchange Online, Teams and PnP.PowerShell modules

```powershell
Install-Module Az.Accounts, ExchangeOnlineManagement, MicrosoftTeams, PnP.PowerShell -Scope CurrentUser
```

> The Security & Compliance PowerShell module is dependent on the ExchangeOnlineManagement `Connect-IPPSSession` cmdlet.

### Connecting to Azure, Exchange, and other services

In order to run all the CISA tests, you need to connect to the Azure, Exchange Online, and other modules.

For a more detailed introduction to these concepts see the [Connect-Maester](connect-maester/readme.md) documentation.

Run the following command to interactively connect to the Azure, Microsoft Graph, Exchange Online, and other modules. A sign-in window will appear for each module.

```powershell
Connect-Maester -Service All
```

### Connecting to GitHub

GitHub is an optional connection for GitHub security tests and is not included in `Connect-Maester -Service All`.
For interactive sessions, use the Maester GitHub App OAuth flow:

```powershell
Connect-Maester -Service Graph,GitHub -GitHubOrganization '<github-organization>'
```

See [Connect to GitHub (optional)](connect-maester/readme.md#connect-to-github-optional) for GitHub App install/approval details and token-based automation options.

### Permissions

Exchange Online implements a [role-based access control model](https://learn.microsoft.com/exchange/permissions-exo/permissions-exo). The controls these cmdlets test require minimum roles of either of the following:

* View-Only Configuration OR
* O365SupportViewConfig

### Installing Azure DevOps PowerShell module

```powershell
Install-Module ADOPS -Scope CurrentUser
```

### Connecting to Azure DevOps

In order to run all the Azure DevOps tests, you need to connect to Azure DevOps.

This is currently not included as part of [Connect-Maester](connect-maester/readme.md) and must be called separately. Run the following command to interactively connect using the Azure DevOps modules. A sign-in window will appear.

Example with PowerShell variable
```powershell
$AdoPSAllowInsecureAPIs = $true
Import-Module ADOPS
Connect-ADOPS -Organization <Name Of DevOps Organization>
```

Example with ArgumentList
```powershell
Import-Module ADOPS -ArgumentList $true
Connect-ADOPS -Organization <Name Of DevOps Organization>
```

> Note: Some of the API endpoints used for Azure DevOps tests use unsupported endpoints.
To allow usage of unsupported endpoints, you must set `$true` in the argumentlist when importing the module, or set a PowerShell variable called "$AdoPSAllowInsecureAPIs" to `$true` before importing the module.
Reference: https://github.com/AZDOPS/AZDOPS/issues/248

### Permissions

Azure DevOps implements a [role-based access control model](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/devops/organizations/security/permissions?view=azure-devops&tabs=preview-page). The controls these cmdlets test require the minimum role of:

* Project-Scoped Users at Organization level

## Next Steps

- Monitoring with Maester
  - [Set up Maester on GitHub](monitoring/github.md)
  - [Set up Maester on Azure DevOps](monitoring/azure-devops.md)
  - [Set up Maester on Azure Container App Jobs](monitoring/azure-container-app-job.md)
- Alerting with Maester
  - [Set up Maester email alerts](alerts/email.md)
  - [Set up Maester Teams alerts](alerts/teams.md)
  - [Set up Maester Slack alerts](alerts/slack.md)
- [Writing Custom Tests](writing-tests/index.mdx)

### Connect to Azure DevOps (optional)

Maester includes an *optional* set of Azure DevOps security tests (AZDO.*).
These tests require the community [`ADOPS`](https://www.powershellgallery.com/packages/ADOPS) PowerShell module and an active connection to your Azure DevOps organization.

Connecting to Azure DevOps is **not** part of `Connect-Maester` and must be done separately:

```powershell
Install-Module ADOPS -Scope CurrentUser
Connect-ADOPS -Organization <your-organization>
```

If the `ADOPS` module is not installed or there is no active connection, the Azure DevOps tests are skipped automatically.

See the [installation guide](../installation.md#installing-azure-devops-powershell-module) for prerequisites and permissions, and the [Azure DevOps tests for Maester](/blog/azuredevops-tests-for-maester) blog post for the full list of available tests.

content.content:
**Per tenant:**
- An **app registration** with the required [Microsoft Graph read permissions](https://maester.dev/docs/installation#permissions) granted with admin consent
- A **workload identity federation service connection** in Azure DevOps pointing to the app registration

### Get Started

Follow the prerequisites above and the [Maester permissions docs](https://maester.dev/docs/installation#permissions) to get your multi-tenant monitoring up and running.
```powershell
Install-Module ADOPS -Scope CurrentUser
Connect-ADOPS -Organization <your-organization>
```

> Some Azure DevOps tests require organization-level permissions such as *Project Collection Administrator* (e.g., AZDO.1030) or tenant-level permissions such as *Azure DevOps Administrator* (e.g., AZDO.1032–1036). See [Manage policies as Administrator](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/devops/organizations/accounts/manage-pats-with-policies-for-administrators?view=azure-devops#prerequisites) and the [installation guide](../installation.md#installing-azure-devops-powershell-module).
### (Optional) Grant permissions to Exchange Online

The Exchange Online role-based access control (RBAC) implementation uses service-specific roles for applications. The configuration below establishes the authorization chain for the app registration you created in the previous steps.

> The Exchange Online permissions are necessary to support tests that validate [Exchange Online configurations](https://maester.dev/docs/installation#installing-azure-and-exchange-online-modules), such as the [CISA tests](https://maester.dev/docs/tests/cisa).

- Open the application you created in the previous step
### (Optional) Grant permissions to Teams

The Teams role-based access control (RBAC) implementation uses service-specific roles for applications. The configuration below establishes the authorization chain for the app registration you created in the previous steps.

> The Teams permissions are necessary to support tests that validate [Teams configurations](https://maester.dev/docs/installation#installing-azure-exchange-online-and-teams-modules).

- Open Roles and administrators
## Before you start

- Maester is installed and you can run `Connect-Maester`. See the [installation guide](../installation.md).
- You have a folder for your own tests, for example `~/maester`. Any empty folder works. Your tests go in a `custom`
  folder inside it, which `New-MtTest` creates, and updating Maester never touches it.

231	### Connect to Azure DevOps (optional)
232	
233	Maester includes an *optional* set of Azure DevOps security tests (AZDO.*).
234	These tests require the community [`ADOPS`](https://www.powershellgallery.com/packages/ADOPS) PowerShell module and an active connection to your Azure DevOps organization.
235	
236	Connecting to Azure DevOps is **not** part of `Connect-Maester` and must be done separately:
237	
238	```powershell
239	Install-Module ADOPS -Scope CurrentUser
240	Connect-ADOPS -Organization <your-organization>
241	```
242	
243	If the `ADOPS` module is not installed or there is no active connection, the Azure DevOps tests are skipped automatically.
244	
245	See the [installation guide](../installation.md#installing-azure-devops-powershell-module) for prerequisites and permissions, and the [Azure DevOps tests for Maester](/blog/azuredevops-tests-for-maester) blog post for the full list of available tests.

input.new_string:
```powershell
Install-Module ADOPS -Scope CurrentUser
Import-Module ADOPS -ArgumentList $true
Connect-ADOPS -Organization <your-organization>
```

Some of the endpoints the tests call are ones `ADOPS` treats as unsupported. `-ArgumentList $true` allows them.
Instead, you can set `$AdoPSAllowInsecureAPIs = $true` before you import the module. See
[AZDOPS issue 248](https://github.com/AZDOPS/AZDOPS/issues/248).

The tests need the **Project-Scoped Users** role at the organization level, at least. Some need more, see
[Connect-Maester advanced](connect-maester-advanced.mdx).

If the `ADOPS` module is not installed or there is no active connection, the Azure DevOps tests are skipped automatically.

See the [Azure DevOps tests for Maester](/blog/azuredevops-tests-for-maester) blog post for the full list of available tests.

## Common questions

**We already have Microsoft Secure Score. Why add this?**
Secure Score is Microsoft's view of recommended settings, and it is worth tracking. Maester adds what Secure Score
does not: tests for your own rules (this group must be in this policy, this app must not have these permissions),
results mapped to the framework you report against, a daily result in your own pipeline with alerts, and the
CIS, CISA, ASD Essential Eight, EIDSCA and ORCA checks side by side with Maester's own.

**We already have a SIEM, Defender and Sentinel.**
Those watch for activity: sign-ins, alerts, attacks in progress. Maester checks configuration: whether the controls
that prevent those attacks are still in place. A weak setting produces no alert until it is exploited.

**It is free. Who supports it?**
Maester is an open-source project maintained by a community of Microsoft security practitioners, with the source
on [GitHub](https://github.com/maester365/maester). There is no vendor support contract. Because it only reads
configuration and runs in your own environment, the operational risk of a fault is low: the worst case is a run that
fails or a test that reports the wrong result, which you can turn off.

---
Installation guide

This page is the reference for installing Maester and the modules its tests use. To go from nothing to your first report, follow Getting started.

Requirements
Section titled “Requirements”
PowerShell 7.4 or later on Windows, Linux or macOS. Windows PowerShell 5.1 is not supported.
An account that can read your tenant’s configuration, such as Global Reader. See Connect-Maester.
Install Maester
Section titled “Install Maester”
PS>Install-Module Maester -AllowPrerelease
Copy

Installs the 3.0 preview, which these docs describe. About the preview

The tests ship inside the module, so there is nothing else to download and no folder to set up. The one module Maester requires, Microsoft.Graph.Authentication, is installed with it.

You need a folder only to change settings or add your own tests. Put a maester-config.json (see Configuration) and a custom folder for your tests (see Writing custom tests) in it, and run Invoke-Maester -Path <folder> or run Maester from that folder.

Upgrading from Maester 2.x? See Upgrading from 2.x.

Update or pin a version
Section titled “Update or pin a version”

Update to the latest release (add -AllowPrerelease for the latest preview):

Update-Module Maester

For scheduled runs, pin a version so that a new release changes your results only when you choose. Read the release notes, then install the version you reviewed:

Install-Module Maester -RequiredVersion <version> -Scope CurrentUser
Optional modules and permissions
Section titled “Optional modules and permissions”

Connect-Maester connects to Microsoft Graph, which is enough for the Entra ID tests and most of the others. The tests for the services below need a module or a connection of their own. When one is missing, its tests are reported as Skipped with the reason, and Connect-Maester shows the command that installs the missing module.

Service	Module	How to connect	Permissions
Azure, Copilot Studio (Dataverse)	Az.Accounts	Connect-Maester	Azure, Dataverse
Exchange Online, Security & Compliance	ExchangeOnlineManagement	Connect-Maester	Exchange Online
Microsoft Teams	MicrosoftTeams	Connect-Maester	Teams
SharePoint Online	PnP.PowerShell, and an app registration whose client ID you pass with -SharePointClientId	Connect to SharePoint Online	SharePoint Online
GitHub	None	Connect to GitHub	The Maester GitHub App, or a token
Azure DevOps	ADOPS	Connect to Azure DevOps	Azure DevOps
Active Directory	None	Connect-Maester -Service ActiveDirectory, see AD connection 

[truncated to 2500 chars]

content.text:
I pushed the changes to PR 2678 as commit `459da6710`. The local site build and the URL contract check pass (2679 of 2679 old URLs still resolve), and every new anchor link resolves. GitHub's CI hasn't run on the commit yet.

**Installation guide** ([installation.mdx](../maester-pr-2678/website/docs/installation.mdx)): it's now a reference page and points readers to Getting started for their first run. It has:
- Requirements, including that Windows PowerShell 5.1 isn't supported.
- Install, plus a new "Update or pin a version" section. The ITSA template tells readers to pin a version, and no page showed how.
- One table for the services that need a module or connection of their own (Azure, Exchange, Teams, SharePoint, GitHub, Azure DevOps, Active Directory): what to install, a link to how to connect, and a link to its permissions.
- `-SharePointClientId`, so Getting started's "Installation covers both" is now true.
- The Exchange roles and the Pester note, kept from the old page.

**Azure DevOps:** the setting that lets the `ADOPS` module call unsupported endpoints, and the minimum role, moved into the [Connect-Maester](../maester-pr-2678/website/docs/connect-maester/readme.md) Azure DevOps section.

**Get started links:** the header button, the homepage button (relabelled from "Quickstart →" to "Get started →") and the 404 page now go to `/docs/getting-started`. The header's "Install" link still goes to Installation.

**Broken links:** six links pointed at Installation anchors that are gone or never existed. They're in `create-entra-app`, the Azure DevOps multi-tenant pipeline page and Connect-Maester advanced, and now point to pages that have the content.

**Maester Cloud:** yes, worth adding, and I've added it to "It is free. Who supports it?". The answer now:
- sends questions and bugs to GitHub issues;
- names Maester Cloud for organisations that need a vendor behind the product. It runs Maester in their own Azure subscription, keeps results over time, alerts on changes, comes with support for setting it up and running it, and funds the open-source project.

I based this on what maester.cloud says today: its support covers the service itself, and enterprise support is only on a waitlist. So I didn't promise support for the open-source module or any service level.

I also changed "it only reads configuration" to "it reads configuration", since `-Privileged` can change a setting.

---
title: Zero Trust Assessment pack
description: Run Microsoft's Zero Trust Assessment from Maester and see each of its results in the Maester report.
sidebar:
  order: 4
---

# Zero Trust Assessment pack

This pack runs Microsoft's [Zero Trust Assessment](https://aka.ms/zerotrust/assessment) and shows each of its
results in the Maester report, next to Maester's own checks. It ships with Maester and does not run unless you
ask for it.

Each assessment result is one row, `ZTA.<assessment test ID>` (for example `ZTA.21770`), with the
assessment's title, risk level (as the severity), description, remediation steps and findings. Results are tagged
`ZeroTrust` and `ZeroTrust.<pillar>` (`ZeroTrust.Identity`, `ZeroTrust.Devices` and so on).

Maester also places each result under the product, feature and security area it is about, such as Entra ID and
Conditional Access, and lists the MITRE ATT&CK techniques its control addresses, so assessment results appear
beside Maester's own checks in the report's product, area and ATT&CK views. The assessment does not record these,
so Maester keeps the mapping in the pack's `taxonomy.json`.

The pack's ID is `maester.zero-trust-assessment`. It needs no `Install-MtPack`: it is part of the Maester module,
and `Get-MtPack` lists it.

## Run it

Install the assessment's module once, connect Maester to the tenant, then name the pack. ZeroTrustAssessment 3.1.0 needs
PowerShell 7.6 or later (Maester itself runs on 7.4); on an older PowerShell the pack is skipped and says so.


```powershell
Install-Module ZeroTrustAssessment -Scope CurrentUser
Connect-Maester
Invoke-Maester -Pack ZTA -SkipBuiltIn    # only the Zero Trust Assessment
Invoke-Maester -Pack ZTA                 # Maester's tests and the assessment
```

You don't run `Connect-ZtAssessment` yourself. The assessment runs in a separate PowerShell process, which can't
use the sign-ins of your session, so Maester signs in there for you (see
[Let Maester run the assessment](#let-maester-run-the-assessment)). After an interactive `Connect-Maester` you
sign in a second time, in the browser, for the assessment. `Connect-Maester` is still needed: it tells the
assessment which tenant to sign in to, and the pack is skipped while Maester is not connected to Graph. If you
read a report you already have (below), you run `Connect-ZtAssessment` and `Invoke-ZtAssessment` yourself first.

The pack is a long-running test, so `Invoke-Maester` leaves it out unless you name it. These also run it:

```powershell
Invoke-Maester -TestId ZTA          # only the Zero Trust Assessment
Invoke-Maester -Suite ZTA              # the same
Invoke-Maester -IncludeLongRunning          # everything, including the assessment
```

The pack itself stays enabled, so naming it is enough; it is the long-running flag that keeps it out of a plain
`Invoke-Maester`. To remove it entirely, set `Packs: [{ "Id": "maester.zero-trust-assessment", "Enabled": false }]`.

To run it on every run, add it to `Selection.TestId` in `maester-config.json`, or set
`Selection.IncludeLongRunning` to `true`. Give it time with `Execution.LongRunningTimeoutSeconds`: the assessment
can take an hour or more on a large tenant.

The pack gets the assessment's results one of two ways.

### Read a report you already have (recommended in CI)

Run the assessment as its own step, then point Maester at the report it wrote:

```powershell
Install-Module ZeroTrustAssessment -Scope CurrentUser
Connect-ZtAssessment
Invoke-ZtAssessment -Path ./zt -NoBrowser
```

```json
{ "GlobalSettings": { "ZeroTrustAssessment.ReportPath": "./zt" } }
```

Then, in a new PowerShell session (the assessment's modules can't share one with Maester's), connect Maester to
the same tenant and run the pack:

```powershell

---
title: Getting started
description: Your first Maester run, how to read the report, and how to go from a one-off check to continuous monitoring.
---

import InstallCommand from '@components/InstallCommand.astro';

# Getting started

This page takes you from nothing to a first report in about fifteen minutes, then shows the steps most teams take
over the following weeks. Each step links to the full guide.

## Before you start

- **PowerShell 7.4 or later** on Windows, Linux or macOS.
- **An account that can read your tenant's configuration.** Global Reader is the usual choice. The first time
  you connect, an admin may need to consent to the Microsoft Graph permissions Maester asks for (see
  [Approval required when connecting](connect-maester/readme.md#approval-required-when-connecting)).

By default Maester asks only for read permissions. It does not change anything in your tenant.

## Step 1: Run your first report

Install Maester, then connect and run it:

<InstallCommand />

```powershell
Connect-Maester
Invoke-Maester
```

`Connect-Maester` connects to Microsoft Graph. That is enough for the Entra ID tests and most of the others. The
Exchange Online, Teams and SharePoint tests need their own PowerShell modules, and SharePoint also needs an app
registration whose client ID you pass with `-SharePointClientId`. [Installation](installation.mdx#optional-modules-and-permissions)
covers both. Then connect to all the services:

```powershell
Connect-Maester -Service All -SharePointClientId '<Client ID>'
Invoke-Maester
```

Tests for a service you have not connected to are reported as **Skipped**, with the reason, so you can tell which
results are missing and why. See [Connect-Maester](connect-maester/readme.md).

## Step 2: Read the report

When the run finishes, Maester writes an HTML report to the `./test-results` folder and, in an interactive session, opens it. Every test appears with one
of these results:

| Result | What it means |
| --- | --- |
| **Passed** | The setting matches what the test expects. |
| **Failed** | The setting does not match. The test explains why and how to fix it. |
| **Investigate** | Maester found something a person should look at; it cannot decide on its own. |
| **Skipped** | The test did not run, for example because a service is not connected, a licence is missing or a permission was not granted. |
| **Error** | The test could not finish, for example because a service returned an unexpected error. |
| **Not run** | The test was left out of this run, for example because your configuration turned it off. The reason is shown. |

Each failed test links to its own page on this site, with the background, the fix and the references.

## Step 3: Fix what matters first

A first report usually has many failures. Do not try to fix them all at once.

1. **Sort by severity.** Start with **Critical** and **High** (see [Severity levels](configuration/severity-levels.md)).
   To run only those tests:

   ```powershell
   Invoke-Maester -Severity Critical, High
   ```

2. **Look for quick wins.** Each test says how much its fix affects users and how much effort it takes. A failure
   with high severity, low user impact and low cost is the best place to start. In an interactive run, the
   **Fix first** panel lists these failures for you.
3. **Record what you accept.** Some failures are deliberate decisions. Turn those tests off in your configuration
   with a reason, so the report shows them as **Not run** with your reason instead of as failures (see the next
   step).

## Step 4: Tell Maester about your tenant

Create a folder for your Maester settings and a `maester-config.json` in it. The most important setting is your
emergency access (break glass) accounts, which many Conditional Access tests depend on:

```json
{
  "GlobalSettings": {
    "EmergencyAccessAccounts": [
      { "Type": "User", "UserPrincipalName": "BreakGlass1@contoso.com" }
    ]
  }
}
```

Then run Maester from that folder, or pass it with `-Path`:

```powershell
Invoke-Maester -Path ./maester
```

When you have decided to accept a failure, add a `TestSettings` row for that test with your reason. Add one only
for a decision that has been made, because the test then stops checking that setting:

```json
{
  "TestSettings": [
    { "Id": "<test ID>", "Enabled": false, "Reason": "<the decision and where it is recorded, for example RISK-042>" }
  ]
}
```

See [Configure Maester](configuration/overview.md) and [Emergency access accounts](configuration/emergency-access-accounts.md).

## Step 5: Choose your baseline

Maester ships several suites: its own tests and the CIS, CISA, ASD Essential Eight, EIDSCA and ORCA suites. Pick the ones that match
the requirements your organisation has to meet. See [Choosing a baseline](choosing-a-baseline.md).

## Step 6: Monitor continuously

A single report shows where you stand today. The value of Maester comes from running it every day, so that a change
that weakens your security is caught within a day instead of at the next audit.

1. Run Maester on a schedule from a pipeline or an Azure service. See [Monitoring with Maester](monitoring/readme.mdx).
2. Send the results to the people who act on them by email, Teams or Slack. See [Maester alerts](alerts/readme.mdx).
3. Export results for a ticketing system or a spreadsheet. See [Exporting results](export-results.md).

## Step 7: Add your own tests

The built-in tests check widely recommended settings. Your organisation also has its own rules: a group that must
always be in a policy, a named location that must exist, an app that must never get more permissions. Write those
rules as [custom tests](writing-tests/index.mdx) and Maester checks them on every run alongside the built-in ones.

## Next steps

- Need support from leadership to roll this out? See [Making the case for Maester](making-the-case.mdx).
- Questions? See the [FAQ](faq.md).

import InstallCommand from '@components/InstallCommand.astro';

# Getting started

This page takes you from nothing to a first report in about fifteen minutes, then shows the steps most teams take
over the following weeks. Each step links to the full guide.

## Before you start

- **PowerShell 7.4 or later** on Windows, Linux or macOS.
- **An account that can read your tenant's configuration.** Global Reader is the usual choice. The first time
  you connect, an admin may need to consent to the Microsoft Graph permissions Maester asks for (see
  [Approval required when connecting](connect-maester/readme.md#approval-required-when-connecting)).

By default Maester asks only for read permissions. It does not change anything in your tenant.

## Step 1: Run your first report

Install Maester, then connect and run it:

<InstallCommand />

```powershell
Connect-Maester
Invoke-Maester
```

`Connect-Maester` connects to Microsoft Graph. That is enough for the Entra ID tests and most of the others. The
Exchange Online, Teams and SharePoint tests need their own PowerShell modules, and SharePoint also needs an app
registration whose client ID you pass with `-SharePointClientId`. [Installation](installation.mdx#optional-modules-and-permissions)
covers both. Then connect to all the services:

```powershell
Connect-Maester -Service All -SharePointClientId '<Client ID>'
Invoke-Maester
```

Tests for a service you have not connected to are reported as **Skipped**, with the reason, so you can tell which
results are missing and why. See [Connect-Maester](connect-maester/readme.md).

### For a comprehensive check, add the Zero Trust Assessment

For the most complete picture of your tenant, also run Microsoft's
[Zero Trust Assessment](packs/zero-trust-assessment.md). It ships with Maester as a pack, and its results appear in
the same report as Maester's own checks, grouped by Zero Trust pillar and placed beside the Maester checks for the
same product and area.

```powershell
Install-Module ZeroTrustAssessment -Scope CurrentUser
Connect-Maester -Service All -SharePointClientId '<Client ID>'
Invoke-Maester -Pack ZTA
```

The assessment needs PowerShell 7.6 or later and asks you to sign in a second time, in the browser. It can take an
hour or more on a large tenant, which is why a plain `Invoke-Maester` leaves it out until you name it. To include it
in every run, see [Run it](packs/zero-trust-assessment.md#run-it).

## Step 2: Read the report

When the run finishes, Maester writes an HTML report to the `./test-results` folder and, in an interactive session, opens it. Every test appears with one
of these results:

| Result | What it means |
| --- | --- |
| **Passed** | The setting matches what the test expects. |
| **Failed** | The setting does not match. The test explains why and how to fix it. |
| **Investigate** | Maester found something a person should look at; it cannot decide on its own. |
| **Skipped** | The test did not run, for example because a service is not connected, a licence is missing or a permission was not granted. |
| **Error** | The test could not finish, for example because a service returned an unexpected error. |
| **Not run** | The test was left out of this run, for example because your configuration turned it off. The reason is shown. |

Each failed test links to its own page on this site, with the background, the fix and the references.

## Step 3: Fix what matters first

A first report usually has many failures. Do not try to fix them all at once.

1. **Sort by severity.** Start with **Critical** and **High** (see [Severity levels](configuration/severity-levels.md)).
   To run only those tests:

   ```powershell
   Invoke-Maester -Severity Critical, High
   ```

2. **Look for quick wins.** Each test says how much its fix affects users and how much effort it takes. A failure
   with high severity, low user impact and low cost is the best place to start. In an interactive run, the
   **Fix first** panel lists these failures for you.
3. **Record what you accept.** Some failures are deliberate decisions. Turn those tests off in your configuration
   with a reason, so the report shows them as **Not run** with your reason instead of as failures (see the next
   step).

## Step 4: Tell Maester about your tenant

Create a folder for your Maester settings and a `maester-config.json` in it. The most important setting is your
emergency access (break glass) accounts, which many Conditional Access tests depend on:

```json
{
  "GlobalSettings": {
    "EmergencyAccessAccounts": [
      { "Type": "User", "UserPrincipalName": "BreakGlass1@contoso.com" }
    ]
  }
}
```

Then run Maester from that folder, or pass it with `-Path`:

```powershell
Invoke-Maester -Path ./maester
```

When you have decided to accept a failure, add a `TestSettings` row for that test with your reason. Add one only
for a decision that has been made, because the test then stops checking that setting:

```json
{
  "TestSettings": [
    { "Id": "<test ID>", "Enabled": false, "Reason": "<the decision and where it is recorded, for example RISK-042>" }
  ]
}
```

See [Configure Maester](configuration/overview.md) and [Emergency access accounts](configuration/emergency-access-accounts.md).

## Step 5: Choose your baseline

Maester ships several suites: its own tests and the CIS, CISA, ASD Essential Eight, EIDSCA and ORCA suites. Pick the ones that match
the requirements your organisation has to meet. See [Choosing a baseline](choosing-a-baseline.md).

## Step 6: Monitor continuously

A single report shows where you stand today. The value of Maester comes from running it every day, so that a change
that weakens your security is caught within a day instead of at the next audit.

1. Run Maester on a schedule from a pipeline or an Azure service. See [Monitoring with Maester](monitoring/readme.mdx).
2. Send the results to the people who act on them by email, Teams or Slack. See [Maester alerts](alerts/readme.mdx).
3. Export results for a ticketing system or a spreadsheet. See [Exporting results](export-results.md).

## Step 7: Add your own tests

The built-in tests check widely recommended settings. Your organisation also has its own rules: a group that must
always be in a policy, a named location that must exist, an app that must never get more permissions. Write those
rules as [custom tests](writing-tests/index.mdx) and Maester checks them on every run alongside the built-in ones.

## Next steps

- Need support from leadership to roll this out? See [Making the case for Maester](making-the-case.mdx).
- Questions? See the [FAQ](faq.md).

  ```powershell

  ```
- **What to expect, from the pack's own page:**
